content: 1. Pulmonary reactions, which may be acute, subacute, or chronic, have been observed in patients treated with nitrofurantoin. If such reactions occur, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate measures should be taken. Pulmonary reactions have been reported as a contributing cause of death in some cases. Chronic pulmonary reactions, such as diffuse interstitial pneumonitis or pulmonary fibrosis, may develop insidiously and are more likely in patients receiving therapy for six months or longer. These reactions are rare, but close monitoring of pulmonary function is warranted in patients on long-term therapy. The benefits of therapy should always be weighed against the potential risks. 2. Hepatic reactions, including hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, chronic active hepatitis, and hepatic necrosis, are rare but have been reported. Fatalities have occurred. Chronic active hepatitis may have an insidious onset, and patients should be periodically monitored for changes in biochemical tests indicative of liver injury. If hepatitis occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate interventions should be initiated. 3. Peripheral neuropathy, which can become severe or irreversible, has been reported in patients taking nitrofurantoin. Fatalities have also been documented. Conditions such as renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 60 mL/min or significantly elevated serum creatinine), anemia, diabetes mellitus, electrolyte imbalance, vitamin B deficiency, and debilitating disease may increase the risk of peripheral neuropathy. Patients on long-term therapy should have their renal function monitored periodically. Rare cases of optic neuritis have also been reported in postmarketing experience. 4. Hemolytic anemia of the primaquine-sensitivity type has been induced by nitrofurantoin. This hemolysis is associated with a glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency in red blood cells, which is more common in certain populations, including 10% of Black individuals and smaller percentages of Mediterranean and Near-Eastern ethnic groups. Hemolysis is an indication to discontinue the drug, and it ceases once the drug is withdrawn. 5. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including nitrofurantoin. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial agents disrupt the normal flora of the colon, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after the last dose. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be initiated as clinically indicated. 6. Patients should be advised to take nitrofurantoin with food, ideally at breakfast and dinner, to enhance tolerance and improve drug absorption. They should complete the full course of therapy but contact their physician if any unusual symptoms occur during treatment. Patients should avoid using antacid preparations containing magnesium trisilicate while taking nitrofurantoin. They should also be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including nitrofurantoin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections like the common cold. Patients should be informed that skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance. 7. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients may develop watery and bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, even two or more months after completing antibiotic therapy. If this occurs, they should contact their physician immediately. 8. Nitrofurantoin should not be prescribed in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication, as this increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 9. Antacids containing magnesium trisilicate reduce the absorption of nitrofurantoin when taken concurrently. This interaction likely occurs due to adsorption of nitrofurantoin onto the surface of magnesium trisilicate. Uricosuric drugs, such as probenecid and sulfinpyrazone, inhibit renal tubular secretion of nitrofurantoin, leading to increased serum levels and potential toxicity, while reducing urinary levels and its efficacy as a urinary tract antibacterial. 10. Nitrofurantoin may cause false-positive results for glucose in the urine when using Benedict's or Fehling's solutions but not with glucose enzymatic tests. 11. Chronic rodent bioassays have shown no evidence of carcinogenicity in certain rat and mouse models. However, nitrofurantoin has demonstrated carcinogenic activity in female B6C3F1 mice, with increased incidences of ovarian tumors and other neoplasms. In male F344/N rats, increased incidences of rare kidney tubular cell neoplasms, bone osteosarcomas, and subcutaneous tissue neoplasms were observed. The relevance of these findings to humans is unknown. 12. Nitrofurantoin has been shown to induce point mutations in certain strains of Salmonella typhimurium and forward mutations in mouse lymphoma cells. It also caused chromosomal aberrations in Chinese hamster ovary cells but not in human cells in culture. The significance of these mutagenicity findings for human therapeutic use is uncertain. 13. High doses of nitrofurantoin in rats caused temporary spermatogenic arrest, which was reversible upon discontinuation of the drug. In healthy human males, doses of 10 mg/kg/day or greater may, in rare cases, cause slight to moderate spermatogenic arrest with a decrease in sperm count. 14. Reproductive studies in rabbits and rats at doses up to six times the human dose have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus. However, a single study in mice at 68 times the human dose reported growth retardation and a low incidence of minor malformations. At 25 times the human dose, no fetal malformations were observed. The relevance of these findings to humans is uncertain. Nitrofurantoin should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. 15. Nitrofurantoin has been detected in trace amounts in human breast milk. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants under one month of age, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering the importance of the drug to the mother. 16. Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated in infants below one month of age. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients under 12 years of age have not been established. 17. Clinical studies of nitrofurantoin did not include sufficient numbers of elderly patients to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. However, spontaneous reports suggest a higher proportion of pulmonary and hepatic reactions, including fatalities, in elderly patients, likely due to long-term therapy and decreased organ function. Renal function should be monitored in elderly patients, as nitrofurantoin is substantially excreted by the kidneys, and impaired renal function increases the risk of toxicity.
